questions.question: In bootstrap resampling, you draw...
options: Values from your sample, with replacement
Values from your sample, without replacement
questions.explanation: A bootstrap sample has the same size as the original and is drawn with replacement from it, so values can repeat or be left out.

questions.question: What does the standard deviation of the bootstrap means estimate?
options: The standard error of the statistic
questions.explanation: The spread of the statistic across resamples imitates its sampling variability, i.e. its standard error.

questions.question: A sample is {4, 8, 6}. Can a bootstrap sample be {8, 8, 8}?
questions.explanation: Drawing with replacement, each draw is 8 with probability 1/3, and (1/3)³ = 1/27 for all three.

questions.question: How is a 95% bootstrap percentile interval formed?
options: The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap statistics
The min and max of the sample
The middle 95% of the original data
questions.explanation: Sort the B bootstrap statistics and take the values that cut off 2.5% in each tail.

questions.question: Which statistic is a good use case for the bootstrap?
options: The mean of normal data (a formula exists)
The median of a skewed sample
The number of rows in a table
questions.explanation: The median has no simple standard-error formula. The bootstrap estimates it directly, and no normality assumption is needed.

questions.question: True or false: bootstrapping 10,000 times makes a sample of 5 people as informative as 10,000 people.
options: False, since resampling reveals variability but adds no new information
False, because B must equal n
questions.explanation: Resampling cannot add information. A sample of 5 stays a sample of 5. More resamples only make the estimate of the bootstrap distribution more stable.
